title: Memory Leaks
learning_outcomes: Explain the main idea behind memory leaks in your own words.
Apply memory leaks to a minimal C example and predict the result.
Identify a relevant boundary, portability assumption, or failure mode.

content.intro: This lesson explores Memory Leaks through an original visual, a compact C example and a check you can perform locally.
content.why_it_matters: Understanding memory leaks helps you reason about C programs rather than relying on trial and error. It also helps you communicate assumptions, write safer code, and debug behavior across toolchains.

content_blocks.title: Dynamic allocation lifecycle
content_blocks.alt_text: Check allocation, use the live allocation, release it once, and never use the old pointer again.
content_blocks.caption: Original learning diagram; use it with the written explanation and compiler-specific checks.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text:
Memory Leaks is studied as part of **Dynamic Memory Management**. Start with the contract: identify the inputs or program state, the rule C applies, and the observable result. Then check the behavior in a small, repeatable example.

In C, details can depend on the selected language standard and implementation. Distinguish defined behavior from unspecified, implementation-defined, or undefined behavior, and consult the cited standard/compiler references when portability matters.

content_blocks.title: Practical reasoning
content_blocks.text: For “Memory Leaks”, write down the preconditions first. Identify valid inputs and boundaries, decide which C rule applies, then choose evidence that would falsify your assumption. Prefer a small test with a clear expected result and compile with diagnostics enabled.

content_blocks.title: Allocated storage
content_blocks.run_instructions: Check allocation results and free each successful allocation exactly once after its last use.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original example, rebuild with the same compiler flags, rerun the same inputs, and compare actual output with the stated result. For time-, platform-, or input-dependent examples, record the environment and do not expect identical values everywhere.
content_blocks.limitations: The CodeLeaf lesson page does not run C code. Compile locally or use a separately deployed, isolated C runner; do not execute arbitrary learner code inside FastAPI.

content_blocks.title: Portability and safety check
content_blocks.text: Use a documented standard mode; treat compiler extensions as extensions, not ISO C guarantees. Check return values, buffer bounds, and object lifetime. This course example is draft material and needs code review on the target toolchain before publication.

task: In a scratch file, create one small example that demonstrates memory leaks. Explain the expected result before running it, compile with warnings enabled, and record one boundary case or portability question.
hints: Reduce the program to the smallest example that still shows the concept.
Write down the input, expected result, and assumptions before running it.
Check the official language/compiler reference and test a boundary case.
expected_output: A short, reproducible C example and explanation showing memory leaks, plus a note about one boundary or portability consideration.
common_mistakes: Treating memory leaks as a rule to memorize rather than a behavior to test.
Ignoring compiler warnings, input validity, or object lifetime.
Assuming behavior observed on one compiler is guaranteed by every C implementation.
summary: Memory Leaks belongs to Dynamic Memory Management.
State the assumptions, verify the smallest example, and test boundaries.
Check the selected language standard and target compiler when portability matters.
